title: JavaScript Event Loop, Microtasks and Macrotasks
commitMessage: docs(notes): add JavaScript Event Loop, microtasks and macrotasks deep dive
content:
# 🔄 JavaScript Event Loop: Microtasks and Macrotasks

JavaScript is a **single-threaded** programming language that can only execute one operation at a time. So how does it work asynchronously (non-blocking)? This is achieved through the **Event Loop** mechanism.

---

## 🧱 Core components:

1. **Call Stack**:
   * The stack of functions currently being executed (LIFO — Last In, First Out).
2. **Web APIs (Browser environment)**:
   * Asynchronous capabilities provided by the browser, such as `setTimeout`, `fetch`, and DOM events.
3. **Microtask Queue**:
   * Results of `Promise.then/catch/finally`, `queueMicrotask`, and `async/await`.
4. **Macrotask / Task Queue**:
   * `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate`, I/O operations.

---

## ⚡ Execution order (Priority rule):

1. All synchronous code on the Call Stack runs to completion.
2. As soon as the Call Stack is empty, the Event Loop picks up and executes all tasks in the **Microtask Queue** in order.
3. After the microtasks finish, **one** Macrotask is taken and executed.
4. The cycle repeats.

> 💡 **Rule**: Microtasks always run before Macrotasks!

title: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit: Why Is Zustand Becoming Popular?
commitMessage: docs(notes): add Zustand vs Redux Toolkit architecture comparison
content:
# 🐻 Zustand vs Redux Toolkit: Which One Should You Choose?

The two most popular tools for managing global state in frontend development are **Redux Toolkit (RTK)** and **Zustand**.

---

## 📊 Comparison:

| Feature | Redux Toolkit | Zustand |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Boilerplate code** | A lot (Slice, Store, Provider, Hooks) | Very little (a single `create` function) |
| **Provider required?** | Yes (`<Provider store={store}>`) | **No!** Used directly |
| **Library size** | ~35-40 KB | **~1-2 KB** (extremely lightweight) |
| **Learning curve** | Moderate | Very fast and intuitive |
| **Async operations** | Requires `createAsyncThunk` | A plain `async/await` function is enough |

---

## 🚀 Conclusion:

* **Zustand** — The fastest, most convenient and lightweight solution for small, medium and many modern large projects.
* **Redux Toolkit** — Used in very large enterprise teams where strict standards are required.

title: JavaScript Closures and Scope
commitMessage: docs(notes): explain JavaScript Closures, lexical environment and practical uses
content:
# 🔒 JavaScript Closures

A **closure** is the ability of an inner function to **remember** the variables of its outer (parent) lexical environment, even after the parent function has finished executing.

---

## 📝 Simple practical example:

```javascript
function createCounter() {
  let count = 0; // Private variable

  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    decrement: () => --count,
    getCount: () => count
  };
}

const counter = createCounter();
console.log(counter.increment()); // 1
console.log(counter.increment()); // 2
console.log(counter.getCount());  // 2
// The count variable cannot be modified directly from the outside!
```

---

## 🎯 Key benefits:
1. **Data Encapsulation (hiding data)**: Creating private variables.
2. **Currying**: Building functions that take their arguments in stages.
3. **Preserving state in callbacks and event handling**.

title: React Performance: useMemo, useCallback and React.memo
commitMessage: docs(notes): add React optimization guide with useMemo, useCallback and React.memo
content:
# ⚡ React Performance Optimization: When Should You Use It?

New developers often wrap every function and variable in `useCallback` or `useMemo`. This actually backfires — it can slow your app down.

---

## 🔍 When to use what?

1. **`React.memo`**:
   * When a component should re-render only if its props change.

2. **`useCallback`**:
   * When passing a function defined inside a component as a prop to child components wrapped in `React.memo`.
   * Otherwise, a new function reference is created on every render and the child re-renders anyway.

3. **`useMemo`**:
   * To cache the results of expensive (heavy) calculations:
   ```tsx
   const filteredList = useMemo(() => {
     return heavyCalculation(items);
   }, [items]);
   ```

title: TypeScript: Interface vs Type Aliases Comparison
commitMessage: docs(notes): add comprehensive TypeScript Interface vs Type comparison guide
content:
# 📘 TypeScript: `interface` vs `type`

In TypeScript, either `interface` or `type` is used to define data structures. They are similar in many ways, but there are important differences.

---

## ⚖️ Key differences:

1. **Declaration Merging (merging interfaces with the same name)**:
   * If an `interface` is declared multiple times with the same name, its fields are merged automatically.
   * With `type`, the name cannot be redeclared (it throws an error).

2. **Unions and Primitives**:
   * With `type` you can define Unions (`type Status = 'pending' | 'success'`) and name primitives.
   * `interface` can only describe Object or Function structures.

---

## 💡 Rule of thumb:
* Use **`interface`** for object shapes and library models,
* Use **`type`** for Unions, Tuples and complex type combinations.

title: CSS Grid and Flexbox: 1D vs 2D Layout Differences
commitMessage: docs(notes): add CSS Flexbox vs Grid architectural decision guide
content:
# 🎨 CSS Flexbox vs CSS Grid

Knowing when to use Flexbox and when to use Grid is one of the most frequently asked questions in modern web design.

---

## 📌 Key difference:

* **Flexbox (1D - one-dimensional)**: Arranges elements along a single axis only — either as a row or as a column.
  * *Best for*: Navbar menus, button groups, elements inside a card.
* **Grid (2D - two-dimensional)**: Arranges elements into cells across both rows and columns at the same time.
  * *Best for*: Full page layouts (Dashboard layout), galleries, complex card collections.

title: Browser Storage: localStorage, sessionStorage and Cookies
commitMessage: docs(notes): add Browser Storage comparison (localStorage, sessionStorage, Cookies)
content:
# 💾 Browser Storage: localStorage vs sessionStorage vs Cookies

There are 3 main ways to store user data in the browser:

---

| Feature | localStorage | sessionStorage | Cookies |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lifetime** | Persists until manually cleared | Until the tab (window) is closed | Until the set Expire time passes |
| **Size** | ~5-10 MB | ~5 MB | ~4 KB |
| **Sent to the server?** | No | No | Yes (sent with every HTTP request) |
| **Security** | Vulnerable to XSS attacks | Vulnerable to XSS attacks | Can be protected from XSS with the `HttpOnly` flag |

title: Clean Code: SOLID and DRY Principles in Frontend Development
commitMessage: docs(notes): add Clean Code and DRY guidelines for frontend engineering
content:
# 🧼 Clean Code Principles in Frontend Development

Writing clean code not only makes teamwork easier, but also prevents bugs when extending the project in the future.

---

## 🎯 4 Golden Rules:

1. **DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)**:
   * Don't repeat the same code in two places. Extract it into a separate function or Custom Hook.
2. **KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid)**:
   * A simple solution is always better than a complex architecture.
3. **Single Responsibility**:
   * A component should do only one thing (for example, `UserCard` should only display the profile, not deal with loading data from the API).
4. **Clear and meaningful naming**:
   * Don't name variables `data`, `item`, or `x`; give them clear names that say what they are (`userData`, `productItem`).

title: Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP and CLS Optimization
commitMessage: docs(notes): add Core Web Vitals optimization guide (LCP, INP, CLS)
content:
# 🚀 Core Web Vitals: A Guide to Improving Site Speed

The 3 key metrics defined by Google for evaluating a website's user experience (UX):

---

1. **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)**:
   * How quickly the main large piece of content (for example, a hero image or a large block of text) becomes visible.
   * *Good score*: < 2.5 seconds.
2. **INP (Interaction to Next Paint)**:
   * How quickly the screen responds when the user clicks a button on the page.
   * *Good score*: < 200 ms.
3. **CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)**:
   * Elements unexpectedly jumping and changing position while the page is loading.
   * *Good score*: < 0.1.
